passage: Tejas squatted on the mud floor of the courtyard beside his wooden bullock cart, three marbles and a cloth ball. "Cart first," he told his sister Nikita, "because the cows will need it." He pushed the cart under the charpai. Then he picked up one marble, held it to the sun and forgot the rest. A goat wandered in through the gate. Tejas dropped the marble and ran after the goat, laughing. When Aaji called them for dinner, the ball and two marbles still lay in the dust. Nikita shook her head and scooped them into the basket.

qa.q: What did Tejas decide to put away first?
qa.a: Tejas decided to put the wooden bullock cart away first, pushing it under the charpai.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when the goat wandered in?
qa.a: He felt excited and playful; the goat was more fun than the marbles, so he dropped his plan and ran after it, laughing.

qa.q: What small step could help Tejas finish tidying next time?
qa.a: Someone could stay beside him and name one toy at a time, so the next thing to put away is always in front of him.

qa.q: How does Nikita see her brother's tidying?
qa.a: She seems a little exasperated but used to it, shaking her head and simply finishing the job by scooping the toys into the basket.

grounding: Illustrates a young child picking what to tidy first by what feels important, then dropping the plan when something more exciting appears.

passage: Rain tapped on the window of the small flat in Valencia. Mateo had two drawings on the table: a red fire truck and a half-coloured dog. "Truck first," he announced to Elif, the neighbour's girl who was visiting. "Trucks are faster." He coloured three wheels black. Then Elif opened a tin of glitter glue. Mateo's eyes went wide. He left the truck, grabbed the dog drawing and squeezed silver glitter all over its tail. "Now the dog is magic!" His mum called out that dinner was ready in five minutes. The truck still had one white wheel.

qa.q: What did Mateo draw on the two sheets?
qa.a: Mateo had a red fire truck and a half-coloured dog.

qa.q: How can you tell that Mateo felt thrilled when the glitter glue appeared?
qa.a: His eyes went wide and he dropped the truck straight away to cover the dog's tail, delighted that it was now magic. ✨

qa.q: What could Mateo's mum do to help him finish the truck another day?
qa.a: She could put the glitter away until the truck's last wheel is coloured, then let the glitter be the fun next step.

qa.q: What is it like for Elif when Mateo switches drawings?
qa.a: Elif probably enjoys it, since her glitter glue made the game more exciting and Mateo now wants to share it.

grounding: Shows a small child ordering tasks by what seems fun or urgent, with the plan switching when something shinier turns up.

passage: At the playschool, tidy-up song had started. Hafsa stood by the block corner and pointed. "First the big blocks, then the small ones," she told Sarita. She carried two big blocks to the shelf, very serious. On the way back she saw the dress-up box open, with a shiny gold crown on top. Hafsa put the crown on her head and twirled. The small blocks stayed on the rug. The teacher knelt down and said, "Queen Hafsa, can the crown help carry blocks?" Hafsa giggled, and together they carried the small blocks, one crown-wearing trip at a time.

qa.q: What did Hafsa plan to tidy first?
qa.a: Hafsa planned to tidy the big blocks first, then the small ones.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she saw the gold crown?
qa.a: She felt delighted and pulled away by it; the shiny crown was more exciting than the tidy-up, so she twirled instead of finishing.

qa.q: Which choice worked well for the teacher, and why?
qa.a: The teacher joined Hafsa's game instead of scolding, turning the crown into part of the tidying so the small blocks got carried after all.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Hafsa's plan?
qa.a: Sarita might find it funny that Hafsa sounded so sure about big blocks first and then left the small ones for a crown.

grounding: Illustrates a young child choosing a tidying order and changing it the moment something shinier catches her eye.

passage: I'm Swati, and last Tuesday I learned something the hard way. After school, Lokesh knocked and asked if I wanted to play cricket in the lane. I had a maths worksheet and a map to colour. I thought, one hour of cricket, then I'll do both. It felt true. We played till the streetlights came on. At home, I ate, then sat with the worksheet. The sums were long division, the slow kind. By nine my eyes kept closing, and the map was still white. Next morning I coloured it in the auto, all scribbly. Now I do the sums first, then cricket.

qa.q: What homework did Swati have that day?
qa.a: Swati had a maths worksheet and a map to colour.

qa.q: Why did Swati feel sure there would be time after cricket?
qa.a: Swati sincerely believed one hour of cricket would leave plenty of time, so Swati felt relaxed and hopeful, not careless.

qa.q: What small change did Swati make afterwards?
qa.a: Swati now does the sums first and plays cricket after, so the hardest part is done while still fresh.

qa.q: How might Lokesh be affected by Swati's new order?
qa.a: Lokesh may have to wait a little longer for a cricket partner, but gets a friend who can stay out without worrying.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild who plays first believing there will be time for homework and learns from a rushed, tired evening.

passage: Class note, Grade 4, Wednesday. Divyansh came to school without his English essay. He told me honestly that he had planned to write it after playing football with his cousin Vikas, and that dinner, a cartoon and then sleep happened first. He was not making excuses; he looked genuinely surprised that the evening had gone. We sat together at break and made a small chart with two columns: "hard work first" and "fun after". He wrote the essay's first paragraph then and there. On Friday he brought the finished essay and a tick on his chart. I will check the chart with him again next week.

qa.q: What did Divyansh forget to bring to school?
qa.a: Divyansh came to school without his English essay.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he explained why the essay was missing?
qa.a: He seemed genuinely surprised and a little sheepish, as if he truly had expected the evening to leave time for writing.

qa.q: How did the note-writer support Divyansh, and what could continue?
qa.a: The note-writer made a simple 'hard work first, fun after' chart with him and got the first paragraph started; checking it weekly helps the habit stick.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel if Divyansh starts doing homework before football?
qa.a: Vikas might feel a bit impatient at first, waiting for Divyansh, but their games can go on without Divyansh getting into trouble.

grounding: Illustrates a child who sincerely thinks there will be time to study after play, with an adult teaching the hard-task-first order.

passage:
Dear Diary, Saturday.
Today was supposed to be easy. Science project due Monday: a model of the water cycle. I said, first I'll finish my kite with Lakshmi, then the project. We flew the kite for AGES. Then it got stuck in the neem tree and we spent forever getting it down. After lunch I felt sleepy and napped. Evening came and I had cotton wool clouds and no glue. Papa had to run to the shop. I finished at 10 pm and my clouds look like wet socks 😔
Tomorrow: project FIRST, kite after.
Santosh

qa.q: What was Santosh's science project?
qa.a: The project was a model of the water cycle.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel by the end of the day?
qa.a: Santosh felt disappointed and tired, finishing at 10 pm with clouds that looked like wet socks.

qa.q: What could Santosh try next time to avoid a late night?
qa.a: Santosh could gather the materials and do the project first in the morning, then fly the kite as a reward.

qa.q: How is Papa affected by Santosh's plan going wrong?
qa.a: Papa had to run to the shop for glue in the evening, so Santosh's late start became extra work for him too.

grounding: Shows a child choosing play first and being taught by a stressful evening that the harder task should come first.

passage: Sit, Shreya, and put that phone face down for a minute. When I was your age, fifteen, my board exams were eight weeks away. Your great-uncle Kishore and I shared a room. Every time a neighbour shouted for help carrying a gas cylinder, Kishore ran. He answered every letter, swept the steps, fixed the radio. He felt so busy, so useful. His history book stayed shut. Three weeks before the exam he sat on the bed and said, "I've done everything except the thing." He made a rule: history from six to eight each morning, errands after. He passed, just about. I still remember his face that day.

qa.q: How far away were the board exams when the story begins?
qa.a: The board exams were eight weeks away.

qa.q: What did Kishore feel when he said, "I've done everything except the thing"?
qa.a: He felt shaken and a little ashamed, realising all his busy helping had pushed his history book aside.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story turned things around for Kishore?
qa.a: His rule of history from six to eight each morning, with errands only after, protected the important work before the small jobs could crowd in.

qa.q: How might Shreya see this story?
qa.a: Shreya might recognise herself in it, since the elder asked her to put her phone face down before telling it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who stays busy with small urgent jobs while important exam revision keeps slipping.

passage: The power cut came at seven, right when Darshan had finally opened his chemistry notes. He lit the emergency lamp, but its battery was low. Then his phone buzzed: Tanuja asking about the class trip money list. He replied. Then the group chat. Then his mother needed him to fetch water before the tank ran dry. Each thing took five minutes and felt like a win. At nine the lamp flickered out. Chemistry, the test on Thursday, had got fifteen minutes. Darshan sat in the dark, annoyed. Next evening he switched the phone off, charged the lamp and did chemistry before anything else.

qa.q: When did the power cut happen?
qa.a: The power cut came at seven.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when the lamp went out at nine?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and frustrated with himself, because chemistry had only got fifteen minutes while the small tasks had eaten the evening.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Every quick reply and small chore felt productive, so the test revision kept sliding; switching the phone off and doing chemistry first fixed it.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Darshan's quick reply?
qa.a: Tanuja probably sees him as helpful and reliable, with no idea that answering her cost him study time.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose messages and small chores feel productive while the important exam revision keeps getting postponed.

passage: Gurpreet's revision timetable was stuck on her bedroom door in Pune: physics, two hours, every afternoon. At four she sat down. Her phone lit up. Ankita wanted a photo of today's notes. Gurpreet sent it. Then she watered her mother's plants because they looked dry. Then she answered three more messages and rearranged her pen stand. By six she felt oddly busy and tired, and the physics chapter was on the same page. "Why is it so loud?" she muttered, looking at the phone. She put it in the kitchen drawer, set a timer for forty minutes and opened the book to page 112.

qa.q: Where was Gurpreet's revision timetable stuck?
qa.a: It was stuck on her bedroom door in Pune.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling at six o'clock?
qa.a: She felt oddly busy and tired but uneasy, because physics had not moved though she had been working all afternoon.

qa.q: Which step helped Gurpreet start revising?
qa.a: Putting the phone in the kitchen drawer and setting a forty-minute timer removed the noisy distractions and gave the revision a clear start.

qa.q: How is Ankita affected by Gurpreet's choices?
qa.a: Ankita gets the notes she wanted quickly, and she may not realise that her small request was one of many that pulled Gurpreet away from physics.

grounding: Illustrates urgent-feeling small tasks and messages crowding out quiet, important exam revision for a teenager.

passage: The hostel common room at eleven at night was full of laptops. Leela had four tabs open: a lab report due tomorrow, an aptitude test for placements, a birthday video for her roommate and her mother's missed call. Yash leaned over. "Which one's first?" "All of them," Leela said. She typed two lines of the report, then switched to the aptitude test, then to the video. At one in the morning nothing was finished. Yash pulled a sticky note from his pocket. "Rank them, one to four. Four might not happen." Leela stared. She wrote the report first and texted her mother goodnight.

qa.q: How many tabs did Leela have open?
qa.a: Leela had four tabs open.

qa.q: Why did Leela find ranking her tasks so hard?
qa.a: She felt pressured by all four and anxious that leaving one undone meant failing someone, so treating all as equal felt safer.

qa.q: What would you advise Leela to do tomorrow?
qa.a: Rank the tasks by deadline and cost, accept that the lowest one may wait, and finish one before switching.

qa.q: What is it like for Yash to watch Leela switch between tasks?
qa.a: Yash seems patient but concerned; he can see nothing is getting finished, so he offers a simple way to rank them.

grounding: Illustrates a college student treating every demand as equally urgent and learning that ranking means accepting something will wait.

passage:
Dear Manjula akka,
Sorry I missed your call again. This semester everything wants me at once. I have two assignments, placement mock interviews on Fridays, my hostel friends' plans, and Amma's calls every night. I kept saying yes to all of it, and last week I submitted a half-done assignment and fumbled a mock interview. My professor wrote "rushed" in red. It stung.
So I made a list and put numbers next to it. Assignments first, then placements. Friends only on Sunday. Amma's call I'll keep short on weekdays. It feels selfish, but at least things are getting done.
Love,
Kavitha

qa.q: What word did the professor write on Kavitha's assignment?
qa.a: The professor wrote "rushed" in red.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel about ranking the commitments?
qa.a: Kavitha felt uneasy and a bit selfish about it, but relieved that things were finally getting done.

qa.q: What could Kavitha try to keep the plan realistic?
qa.a: Kavitha could review the numbered list each week and tell friends and Amma in advance when there is free time, so the plan feels fair.

qa.q: How might Manjula akka see this letter?
qa.a: Manjula akka may feel understanding and proud that Kavitha is sorting out priorities, even though it means fewer calls.

grounding: Shows a college student juggling assignments, placement prep, friends and family who learns that ranking means leaving something undone.

passage: So you want the story of my second year? Okay. I'm Ayesha, and in second year I believed that if I was a good person, I'd do everything. Coding practice for placements, two group projects, my cousin Arohi's wedding prep, calls home. My calendar looked like a rainbow exploded. I'd start coding, get a wedding message, switch, then feel guilty and open a project. By exam week I had three unfinished things and a cold. My mentor asked me one question: "If only one thing could be excellent this month, which?" Placements. I picked it, told Arohi I'd help at the wedding but not plan it, and I survived.

qa.q: What was the one question Ayesha's mentor asked?
qa.a: "If only one thing could be excellent this month, which?"

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling during those busy weeks?
qa.a: Ayesha felt guilty and overwhelmed, switching from one task to another whenever a message came in.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Ayesha, and why?
qa.a: Choosing placements as the one thing to be excellent and limiting the wedding role gave Ayesha a clear ranking to act on.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when Ayesha offers to help but not plan?
qa.a: Arohi might feel a little disappointed at first, but likely grateful that Ayesha was honest about what was possible.

grounding: Illustrates a student treating assignments, placements and family as equally pressing until learning to rank them.

subtype: Saying no to protect the main goal [Actor]
passage: In the small block office at Sangli, Usha was drafting the tender papers for the new water tank. They were due at the district office by Friday noon. On Wednesday morning Saurabh, from accounts, came in with a folder. "Can you redo the staff picnic budget in a nicer format? Won't take long." Usha felt her throat tighten. He was friendly, and saying no felt rude. She took a breath. "Not this week, Saurabh. The tender is due Friday. I can look at it Monday." He blinked, then nodded. Usha felt guilty for an hour, then submitted the tender on Thursday evening, a day early.

qa.q: When were the tender papers due?
qa.a: They were due at the district office by Friday noon.

qa.q: What did Usha feel when Saurabh asked for the favour?
qa.a: She felt tense and a bit guilty, because he was friendly and saying no seemed rude.

qa.q: What would you advise Usha to do the next time a small request comes in during a deadline?
qa.a: Say no politely, give the reason and offer a later time, as she did by promising to look at it on Monday.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see Usha's refusal?
qa.a: He seems briefly surprised but accepting; he blinked and nodded, since she gave a clear reason and a later date.

grounding: Shows a young professional declining a small request to protect time for a deadline-critical task, despite feeling guilty.

subtype: Saying no to protect the main goal [Actor]
passage: Javier had one job that week at the design studio in Lisbon: finish the client presentation by Thursday at nine. On Monday, Aiko from the events team messaged him. "Can you make posters for the office quiz night? 🙂" He liked Aiko and loved quiz night. He opened a blank poster file, then closed it. The slides were half done. He wrote back: "I'd love to, but my Thursday deadline has to come first. Could I help next month?" He stared at the screen, feeling like a bad teammate. Aiko replied, "Totally fair!" Javier blocked Tuesday and Wednesday mornings for slides and delivered on time.

qa.q: What was Javier's one job that week?
qa.a: He had to finish the client presentation by Thursday at nine.

qa.q: How did Javier feel after sending his reply?
qa.a: He felt guilty, like a bad teammate, even though he had politely explained his deadline.

qa.q: What step helped Javier protect the main goal after saying no?
qa.a: He blocked Tuesday and Wednesday mornings for the slides, so the saved time went straight to the important work.

qa.q: What is it like for Aiko to receive Javier's no?
qa.a: She seems fine with it and replies "Totally fair!", since he explained why and offered to help next month.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional turning down a low-value request so the deadline-critical work gets protected time.

subtype: Saying no to protect the main goal [Actor]
passage: The hospital records department was quiet at four. Manjula had until Friday to finish the audit files the inspection team needed. Parveen, a senior nurse, leaned into her cubicle. "Manjula, could you reorganise our ward's old leave register? It's such a mess." Manjula looked at the stack of audit folders, twenty-three still to check. Her stomach dropped; Parveen had been kind to her since her first day. "I can't this week," Manjula said. "The audit is due Friday. Can I help on Monday?" Parveen paused, then shrugged. "Fine, Monday." Manjula checked eight folders before six and felt steadier, though the guilt lingered.

qa.q: How many audit folders were still to check?
qa.a: Twenty-three audit folders were still to check.

qa.q: Why did Manjula's stomach drop when Parveen asked?
qa.a: She felt anxious and guilty about refusing someone who had been kind to her since her first day.

qa.q: What worked about Manjula's reply?
qa.a: She said no clearly, named the audit deadline and offered Monday, which protected her time while keeping the relationship.

qa.q: How does Parveen react to Manjula's answer?
qa.a: Parveen pauses, then shrugs and accepts Monday; she seems a little put out but not offended.

grounding: Shows a young professional declining a low-value request to protect a deadline, with the guilt it brings.

passage: People ask how I stopped drowning at work. I'm Anirban. Two years ago my to-do list had forty-one items. Every night I'd look at it and feel sick. My flatmate Santosh watched me one Sunday and said, "Just pick three things for the week. Only three." I laughed, but I tried it. First week: finish the vendor report, call Baba about his tests, run twice. I wrote them on an index card and stuck it by the kettle. Every evening I looked at it while the water boiled. By Friday two were done and the run happened once. That felt like winning, not failing.

qa.q: How many items did Anirban's to-do list once have?
qa.a: Anirban's to-do list had forty-one items.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel about his long list before he tried the top three?
qa.a: Anirban felt sick and overwhelmed looking at it every night.

qa.q: Which part of Anirban's method makes the evening check easy?
qa.a: Sticking the index card by the kettle meant Anirban saw the three outcomes every evening while the water boiled, without needing to remember.

qa.q: How might Santosh see the change in Anirban?
qa.a: Santosh probably feels pleased and a bit proud that the simple advice helped Anirban stop feeling crushed by work.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing three important outcomes for the week, writing them down and checking them each evening.

passage: I share an office with Eshaan at the logistics firm, and I've noticed a change since spring. Every Monday at nine he takes a yellow card and writes three lines. I once saw it: "Ship Pune order. Fix invoice error. Mentor Preeti." Every evening before leaving, he looks at the card, ticks something or frowns, and puts it back under his keyboard. His desk used to be buried in sticky notes. Now it's mostly clear. Preeti told me he gave her a full hour on Wednesday, the first time anyone had. I can't know how he feels inside, but he seems calmer.

qa.q: Where does Eshaan keep his yellow card?
qa.a: He puts it back under his keyboard.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be feeling now that he uses the three-line card?
qa.a: He seems calmer and more in control, judging by his clear desk and steady evening check.

qa.q: What could the colleague try if they want the same results?
qa.a: They could write their own three outcomes on Monday and check them each evening, instead of keeping many sticky notes.

qa.q: How is Preeti affected by Eshaan's new habit?
qa.a: Preeti benefits directly, getting a full hour of mentoring on Wednesday because she was one of his three priorities.

grounding: An observer describes a colleague who picks three weekly outcomes, writes them down and checks them each evening.

passage:
Monday. Chetan's notebook held a list of twenty-two tasks for the week at the bank branch. By Tuesday night he had crossed off six small ones and none of the big ones. He felt heavy.
Wednesday. Zeenat, his team lead, showed him her card: three outcomes, nothing else. That evening Chetan tore out a fresh page and wrote: close the loan file audit, train the new cashier, send the quarterly report. He checked it before sleeping and moved one step forward on each.
Next Monday. Chetan wrote three new lines. By Friday all three had ticks, and the long list felt less like guilt.

qa.q: How many tasks were on Chetan's first list?
qa.a: Chetan's notebook held a list of twenty-two tasks for the week.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on Tuesday night?
qa.a: He felt heavy and discouraged because he had only crossed off small tasks and none of the big ones.

qa.q: Which change worked for Chetan, and why?
qa.a: Writing only three outcomes and checking them each evening kept his attention on what mattered, so all three were done the next week.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see Chetan's progress?
qa.a: Zeenat would likely feel pleased that sharing her simple card helped her team member finish the important work.

grounding: Shows over days how a young worker moves from a long list to three weekly outcomes checked each evening.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: Come here, Jyoti, and leave that chart for a moment. When your mother, Leela, was ten, she had to make a solar system chart for school. The chart paper was huge and white. She stood in front of it for an hour, not drawing, just staring. Then she went and played with the calf. I, her grandmother, found her crying behind the shed. "It's too big, Nani." So we cut it into a plan. First only the sun, in the corner, big and yellow. That was all for day one. The next day, Mercury and Venus. By Saturday, all eight planets. She still has it.

qa.q: What chart did Leela have to make?
qa.a: Leela had to make a solar system chart for school.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when her grandmother found her behind the shed?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and hopeless, crying because the chart seemed too big to do.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Leela start?
qa.a: Deciding to draw only the sun on day one gave her a small first piece, which made the big chart feel doable.

qa.q: How did the grandmother see Leela's crying?
qa.a: The grandmother saw that Leela was frozen by the size of the task, not lazy, so she helped break it into small steps.

grounding: An elder tells how a child froze in front of a big chart until she was given a small first piece to do.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: The summer holiday homework had to be finished by Monday, and it was Saturday. Pooja, eleven, sat at the kitchen table in their two-room flat while her little brother banged pots on the floor. Her history chapter was twenty pages. She flipped through it, sighed and went to the window. Then to the fridge. Then to the window again. Her cousin Lavanya, visiting for the weekend, sat beside her. "Just the first two pages. Find three dates." Pooja underlined 1757, 1857 and 1905. It took ten minutes. "Okay, two more pages," she said, a little surprised, and kept going despite the noise.

qa.q: How many pages was Pooja's history chapter?
qa.a: Her history chapter was twenty pages.

qa.q: Why did Pooja keep going to the window and the fridge?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed by the size of the chapter, so wandering around was a way to escape a task that seemed impossible.

qa.q: What small step helped Pooja get started?
qa.a: Lavanya's suggestion to read just two pages and find three dates gave her a first piece she could finish in ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel after seeing Pooja keep going?
qa.a: Lavanya would likely feel pleased and relieved that her small suggestion got her cousin moving.

grounding: Illustrates a child who sees only the size of a long chapter and wanders off until given a small first piece.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: Sunaina's science project chart was propped against the sofa in their Bhopal flat, still blank. It needed a drawing, labels, a table and a paragraph about plant cells. She looked at it, picked up a pencil and put it down. "I'll do it after dinner," she said. After dinner she went to watch her brother Hrithik play carrom. At nine, Hrithik saw her staring at the blank chart again. "What's the first thing?" he asked. "I don't know. All of it." He handed her a ruler. "Draw the border." She drew it. Then a big circle for the cell. By ten, the labels were done.

qa.q: What was the science project chart about?
qa.a: It needed a drawing, labels, a table and a paragraph about plant cells.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's picking up and putting down the pencil suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt stuck and overwhelmed, seeing the whole chart at once with no idea where to start.

qa.q: How did Hrithik help, and what could Sunaina do alone next time?
qa.a: He asked for the first thing and gave her one tiny task, drawing the border; next time she could name that first small step herself.

qa.q: What is it like for Hrithik to see his sister stuck?
qa.a: Hrithik seems to understand and want to help, calmly handing her a ruler rather than telling her off.

grounding: Shows a child frozen by a big project chart until someone points her to a tiny first step.

passage:
Arohi: "Done! Study plan for the week."
Darshan: "Show me."
Arohi: "Monday, study. Tuesday, study. Wednesday, study."
Darshan: "Study what?"
Arohi: "Maths. Everything. I'll figure it out."
Darshan: "Remember last week? You sat with your book open for an hour and texted me memes."
Arohi: "That's because I didn't know where to start."
Darshan: "So start with something your hands can do. Like, chapter three, sums one to five."
Arohi: "That's so small."
Darshan: "Small is good. You'll actually do it."
Arohi: "Fine. Monday: chapter three, sums one to five. Tuesday: six to ten."
Darshan: "Now it's a plan 👍"
Arohi: "Ugh. You're right."

qa.q: What did Arohi's first plan say for Monday?
qa.a: The first plan said "Monday, study."

qa.q: How did Arohi feel sitting with the book open last week?
qa.a: Arohi felt lost and stuck, not knowing where to start, so the memes were an escape.

qa.q: What would you advise Arohi to keep doing?
qa.a: Write each day's plan as a specific action, like a numbered set of sums from one chapter, so the starting point is obvious.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Arohi's first plan?
qa.a: Darshan sees it as too vague to act on, and gently teases Arohi into making it concrete.

grounding: A dialogue shows a teenager whose vague study plan leaves no place to start until it becomes a concrete first action.

passage: I'm Jomon, and in Class Nine I wrote "Study physics" on a sticky note and put it above my desk. Every evening I sat down, looked at it and felt blank. Study what? Which chapter? I'd flip pages and end up drawing in the margins. My brother Gautam, who was in college, saw the note and laughed. "That's not a plan, that's a wish." He took the note and wrote: "Read page 45. Solve question 2." I did it in twenty minutes. The next day I wrote my own: "Solve questions 3 and 4." Small, but I finally knew where to put my pencil.
